items.sampleAnswer:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to complain about a laptop (order no. 48213) which I purchased from your website on 2 March. When the parcel arrived a week later, the screen was badly cracked and the device would not switch on.

I contacted your customer service team immediately, attaching photographs of the damage. Not only have I received no reply, but my two follow-up calls were also cut off before I could speak to anyone. Frankly, I find this level of service unacceptable from a company with your reputation.

I would therefore ask you to arrange collection of the faulty laptop and either replace it or issue a full refund. Given that I have already waited three weeks, I expect a response within five working days. Should I not hear from you by then, I will have no choice but to take the matter further.

I look forward to your prompt reply.

Yours faithfully,
Linh Tran

items.sampleAnswer:
Hi Sam,

Congratulations on the job offer! I can totally understand why you're torn, though. Leaving the people you love is never easy, especially when you've lived in the same place your whole life.

That said, opportunities like this don't come along every day. Apart from the higher salary, you'd gain experience that could open doors later in your career. On the other hand, moving somewhere new can be lonely at first, and it might take a while before you feel settled.

If I were in your shoes, I'd probably accept it. The city is only two hours away by train, so you could come back most weekends, and video calls make it much easier to stay in touch than it used to be. What's more, if it really doesn't work out, you can always move back – but you might regret it for years if you never try.

Let me know what you decide, and good luck!

All the best,
Mai

Dear Ms Harper,

I am writing to apply for the position of festival assistant, which I saw advertised on your website last week. I am a second-year business student and a passionate music fan, and I believe I would be well suited to the role.

Last summer I worked as a volunteer at a local food festival, where I was responsible for directing visitors and dealing with enquiries. This taught me how to stay calm under pressure and solve problems quickly, particularly when things did not go according to plan. In addition, I speak fluent English and Vietnamese and have a good working knowledge of French, which would be useful when assisting international performers and guests.

What appeals to me most about this position is the chance to see how a large event is organised behind the scenes. I am hard-working, reliable and happy to work long or irregular hours.

I am available from 15 June until the end of August and would be pleased to attend an interview at your convenience.

Yours sincerely,
Duc Nguyen

items.prompt: 'Social media does more harm than good to young people.' Write an essay giving your opinion.
items.promptVi: 'Mạng xã hội gây hại nhiều hơn lợi cho giới trẻ.' Hãy viết bài luận nêu ý kiến của bạn.
items.sampleAnswer:
Social media has become an inseparable part of teenage life, and its effects are hotly debated. While it undoubtedly brings some benefits, I would argue that, for many young people, the disadvantages outweigh them.

The most serious concern is mental health. Research suggests that heavy users are more likely to experience anxiety and low self-esteem, largely because they constantly compare themselves with carefully edited images of other people's lives. Moreover, endless scrolling can disrupt sleep, which in turn affects concentration at school.

Admittedly, social media allows young people to stay in touch with friends and find communities of people who share their interests. For teenagers who feel isolated, this can be genuinely valuable. However, online contact is no substitute for face-to-face friendship, and cyberbullying means that many young people never feel completely safe.

Finally, it is worth considering how much time is lost. Hours spent online could be used for sport, hobbies or rest.

In conclusion, although social media is not harmful in itself, the way it is designed encourages overuse. Unless young people learn to use it in moderation, it is likely to do more harm than good.

items.prompt: Some people believe that individuals can do little to protect the environment and that only governments can make a real difference. Write an essay giving your opinion.
items.promptVi: Có người cho rằng cá nhân chẳng làm được gì nhiều để bảo vệ môi trường, chỉ chính phủ mới tạo ra thay đổi thật sự. Hãy viết bài luận nêu ý kiến.
points: the power of laws and regulations
items.sampleAnswer:
It is often claimed that environmental problems are so vast that only governments have the power to solve them. While I accept that political action is essential, I do not believe individuals are powerless.

There is no doubt that governments have tools that ordinary people lack. By introducing laws on pollution, investing in public transport and taxing activities that damage the planet, they can change the behaviour of millions of people at once. Without such measures, individual efforts alone would never be enough.

Nevertheless, governments rarely act unless they feel pressure from the public. Every time consumers choose products with less packaging, cycle instead of driving, or cut down on meat, they send a clear message to businesses and politicians. Small actions, multiplied across a population, can have a considerable impact.

Another point worth making is that individuals influence each other. Someone who starts recycling or repairing rather than replacing things often inspires friends and family to do the same.

To sum up, real progress depends on both. Governments must lead, but it is ordinary citizens who create the demand for change in the first place.

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to enquire about the two-week English and Outdoor Adventure course advertised on your website, which I am considering taking in July.

First of all, I would be grateful if you could tell me how students are placed in classes. My English is at an upper-intermediate level, and I would like to know whether there is a placement test and how many students there are in each group.

I would also appreciate some information about accommodation. Your website mentions both host families and a student residence, but it does not explain the difference in cost or whether meals are provided.

Finally, could you clarify exactly what the course fee includes? In particular, I would like to know whether equipment for activities such as kayaking and hill walking is provided, and whether there are any additional charges for excursions.

Thank you in advance for your help. I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully,
Hoa Pham

items.sampleAnswer:
In many countries, students graduate with enormous debts, and this has led to calls for university education to be made free. Although the idea is attractive, I believe it would be fairer to make it affordable rather than completely free.

The strongest argument in favour of free tuition is equality. Talented young people from poorer families are often discouraged from applying because they fear the debt. Removing fees would ensure that ability, not wealth, determines who gets a degree.

On the other hand, universities are extremely expensive to run, and if students paid nothing, the entire cost would fall on taxpayers. This includes people who never went to university themselves and may earn far less than graduates do.

Furthermore, not every student needs the same support. A system of grants for low-income students, combined with loans that are only repaid once graduates earn a reasonable salary, would protect those most in need without placing an unfair burden on everyone else.

In conclusion, access to higher education must not depend on family income. However, a targeted approach seems both more realistic and more just than making university free for all.

Dear Mr Collins,

I am writing to express my disappointment with my recent stay at the Seaview Hotel from 10 to 14 August.

Your website describes the hotel as 'a peaceful retreat just steps from the beach', with 'newly renovated rooms and sea views'. In reality, the hotel is located beside a busy main road, and it took us fifteen minutes to walk to the beach. Our room, far from being renovated, had a broken air-conditioning unit and stained carpets, and the only view was of the car park.

What upset us even more was the attitude of the staff. When we asked to change rooms, the receptionist simply told us that the hotel was full and that nothing could be done. No apology was offered at any point.

I strongly believe that your website should be updated so that future guests are not similarly misled. I would also expect some form of compensation, such as a partial refund, in recognition of the inconvenience we experienced.

I look forward to your reply.

Yours sincerely,
Thu Le

Since the pandemic, working from home has gone from being a rare privilege to a normal arrangement for millions of people. In my view, it offers clear advantages, but only when it is combined with some time in the office.

As far as productivity is concerned, many employees report that they get more done at home, where there are fewer interruptions and no time is wasted commuting. Employers also benefit, since they can reduce the cost of office space and recruit staff who live further away.

Working from home can also improve work–life balance. Parents, for example, find it easier to fit work around their children's schedules. Having said that, the boundary between work and personal life can easily become blurred, and some people end up working longer hours than before.

The main drawback, however, is the loss of human contact. New employees in particular learn a great deal simply by being around experienced colleagues, and spontaneous conversations often lead to the best ideas.

Overall, I believe a hybrid model, in which staff spend part of the week at home and part in the office, offers the best of both worlds.

Rising levels of obesity and diabetes have prompted several governments to introduce taxes on sugary drinks and junk food. Although such taxes are controversial, I believe they can play a useful role if they are introduced carefully.

The main argument in their favour is that price affects behaviour. When the cost of fizzy drinks went up in some countries, sales fell noticeably, and manufacturers even reduced the sugar content of their products to avoid the tax. In this sense, the policy changed not only what people bought but also what companies produced.

Critics, however, point out that these taxes hit poorer families hardest, since they spend a larger share of their income on food. This is a fair concern, but it can be addressed by using the money raised to make fruit and vegetables cheaper or to fund sports facilities in low-income areas.

It should also be remembered that taxes alone will not solve the problem. Education about nutrition and clearer food labelling are equally important.

In conclusion, a tax on unhealthy food is not a complete solution, but as part of a wider strategy it could make a real difference to public health.

A Month Without My Phone? Challenge Accepted… Maybe

Be honest: how many times have you checked your phone today? If you're anything like me, you've probably lost count. My phone is my alarm clock, my map, my bank and my main way of keeping in touch with friends, so the idea of giving it up for a month sounds terrifying.

The practical side would undoubtedly be the hardest part. How would I pay for things, find my way around an unfamiliar part of the city or hear about last-minute changes to my classes? I suspect I'd end up borrowing my flatmate's phone more often than I'd like to admit.

And yet, part of me is curious. Without constant notifications, I might actually finish the books I keep starting, sleep better and pay proper attention to the people I'm with. What I miss most from my childhood is that feeling of being bored – and boredom, after all, is often where creativity begins.

So, could I do it? Probably not for a whole month. But a phone-free weekend? That's a challenge I'm ready to take on.

The Place That Surprised Me Most

When my friends suggested a weekend in Quy Nhon, I wasn't exactly thrilled. I had barely heard of the place, and I assumed it would be just another quiet coastal town with little to do. How wrong I was!

The first surprise was the beaches. Unlike the crowded resorts I'd visited before, the bays around Quy Nhon were almost empty, with water so clear that you could see fish swimming around your feet. The second was the food. The seafood was not only incredibly fresh but also remarkably cheap, and the locals we met were only too happy to recommend their favourite street stalls.

What impressed me most, though, was the sense of history. Just outside the town stand ancient Cham towers, nearly a thousand years old, which we explored at sunset with hardly another tourist in sight.

Would I recommend it? Absolutely – but go soon. Now that new hotels are springing up along the coast, it may not stay a hidden gem for much longer.

The Day I Learned to Say 'No'

In my first year at university, I said yes to everything. Join the drama club? Of course. Help organise the charity concert? Why not? Take on extra shifts at the café? Sure. I genuinely believed that the busier I was, the more successful I would become.

It was only when exam season arrived that I realised how much I had taken on. I was sleeping five hours a night, rushing from one commitment to the next, and doing everything badly. Eventually, I fell ill the week before my most important exam, which I ended up having to retake in the summer.

Looking back, the problem wasn't that I was lazy or disorganised; it was that I couldn't bear to disappoint anyone. What I eventually understood is that saying no to some things is the only way to say yes properly to others.

So here's my advice: before you agree to anything, ask yourself whether you really have the time and energy. If the answer is no, be honest. People are far more understanding than you think.

The Man Who Fixes Everything

If you walk past the corner of Tran Phu Street on a Sunday morning, you'll probably see a queue of people holding broken radios, bicycles and electric fans. At the front of it, you'll find Mr Hai, a retired engineer who has spent the last six years repairing things for free.

It all started when his neighbour's old fan stopped working and she couldn't afford a new one. Mr Hai fixed it in ten minutes, and word quickly spread. Today he repairs dozens of items every week, and he has recently started teaching teenagers how to do the repairs themselves.

The impact has been remarkable. Not only has he saved local families a great deal of money, but he has also kept huge amounts of electronic waste out of landfill. Perhaps more importantly, his Sunday workshop has become a place where neighbours who would never otherwise have met sit and chat while they wait.

Homework: Helpful Habit or Pointless Chore?

Ask any group of students what they think of homework and you'll hear a chorus of complaints. But is homework really a waste of time, or do we simply dislike anything that eats into our free time?

In theory, homework serves a clear purpose. It gives students the chance to practise what they have learned, develop independent study skills and identify what they haven't understood before the next lesson. Without some practice outside the classroom, much of what we learn would quickly be forgotten.

The problem is that homework is not always set with this purpose in mind. Too often, students are given large amounts of repetitive exercises that take hours to complete but teach very little. When tasks pile up from several teachers at once, the result is exhaustion rather than learning.

So what's the answer? Rather than abolishing homework altogether, schools should focus on quality over quantity. Short, meaningful tasks – reading, research or creative projects – would be far more effective. If homework were planned this way, I suspect far fewer students would see it as a waste of time.

When I joined my company's volleyball team two years ago, I could barely serve the ball over the net. Today, training sessions are the highlight of my week – and not just because I've finally learned to serve.

The physical benefits are obvious. Team sports combine running, jumping and quick changes of direction, which improve fitness far more than an hour on a treadmill. Better still, you're having so much fun that you hardly notice how hard you're working.

The real value, however, lies elsewhere. Playing in a team teaches you to communicate under pressure, to trust others and to handle both victory and defeat gracefully. I've also made some of my closest friends on the court, people I would never have met otherwise.

If you're thinking of giving it a go, my advice is simple: don't worry about being bad at first. Most amateur clubs welcome beginners, and nobody expects you to be an expert. Look for a team that trains at a convenient time, turn up with an open mind, and you may well find that, like me, you never want to stop.

At first glance, 'The Last Lighthouse' seems an unlikely film to become a word-of-mouth success. Set almost entirely on a remote island, it follows an elderly lighthouse keeper whose lonely routine is disrupted when a young engineer arrives to install an automated system that will make his job unnecessary.

What begins as a tense relationship gradually develops into an unexpected friendship, and the director handles this shift beautifully. There are no dramatic plot twists; instead, the film relies on small gestures and long silences, supported by breathtaking photography of the stormy coastline.

What really made me think was the way the film explores technology and work. It raises difficult questions about what happens to people when machines replace them, yet it never feels like a lecture. I left the cinema thinking about my grandparents and how much the world has changed during their lifetimes.

Admittedly, the slow pace will not suit everyone. However, if you enjoy thoughtful, character-driven stories, I would highly recommend it. Just make sure you see it on a big screen.

The menu is short but carefully chosen, focusing on traditional dishes rarely found in tourist restaurants. The caramelised fish in a clay pot was rich and full of flavour, while the banana flower salad provided a refreshing contrast. Portions were generous, and the prices were surprisingly reasonable given the quality.

Service was warm and attentive, if a little slow at busy times. Our waiter took the time to explain the origins of each dish, which made the meal feel even more special.

I picked up 'Small Steps' expecting a light holiday read. Instead, I found one of the most honest novels about growing up that I have ever come across.

The story follows Mia, a nineteen-year-old who drops out of university after her first term and returns, embarrassed, to her small hometown. Over the course of a year, she works in her aunt's bakery, reconnects with old friends and slowly works out what she really wants from life.

What I liked most was how realistic it felt. Mia is neither a heroine nor a victim; she makes poor decisions, gets things wrong and occasionally behaves selfishly, yet you can't help caring about her. The dialogue is sharp and often very funny, too.

If I had one criticism, it would be that the middle section drags slightly, with a romantic subplot that adds little to the story.

That said, I would strongly recommend it to anyone who feels pressure to have their whole life planned out. It is a reassuring reminder that taking a different path is not the same as failing.

The idea is simple but clever. Whenever you want to concentrate, you plant a virtual tree and set a timer. If you leave the app to check messages, your tree dies. Over time, your focused sessions grow into a colourful forest, which is surprisingly motivating.

The app's greatest strength is how easy it is to use, and the statistics showing how much time you've spent focusing are genuinely useful. It also lets you study together with friends, which adds a bit of friendly competition. On the downside, the free version contains rather a lot of adverts, and some of the extra features feel unnecessary.

Is it worth paying for? In my opinion, yes. The premium version costs less than a cup of coffee, and the difference it has made to my concentration is well worth the price.

Report on the College Library

Introduction
The aim of this report is to assess the current state of the college library and to recommend ways in which it could be improved. It is based on a survey of 120 students and interviews with library staff.

Strengths
Most students value the library as a quiet place to study, and the staff were frequently described as friendly and helpful. The online catalogue was also praised for being easy to use.

Problems

Staff Travel Report

This report outlines how employees currently travel to the office and suggests measures that could encourage more environmentally friendly options. The findings are based on an online questionnaire completed by 85 members of staff.

Current situation
At present, around 60% of employees drive to work, usually alone. Approximately 25% use public transport, while only a small minority cycle or walk.

The most frequently mentioned reason for driving was convenience, particularly among staff with young children. In light of these findings, I would recommend the following. Firstly, the company should install covered bicycle racks and a changing room with showers. Secondly, a car-sharing scheme could be introduced, with reserved parking spaces for those taking part. Finally, it would be worth discussing with the local council whether a bus stop could be added closer to the office. Exploring Da Lat on a Budget: A Report for Young Visitors

Introduction
This report is intended to help young travellers make the most of Da Lat without spending a fortune. It covers accommodation, food, activities and some practical tips.

Accommodation and food
The town has a wide range of hostels, many of which offer dormitory beds for under ten dollars a night, including breakfast. As for food, the night market is by far the best option. Visitors can try local specialities such as grilled rice paper and warm soy milk for very little money.

Activities
Many of the best experiences are free or almost free. Walking around Xuan Huong Lake at sunrise is highly recommended, as is a visit to the old railway station. For those who enjoy the outdoors, the pine forests surrounding the town offer excellent hiking trails, although it is advisable to go with a local guide.

Practical advice
It is worth remembering that Da Lat is considerably cooler than the rest of Vietnam, so visitors should bring a warm jacket. Renting a motorbike is cheap, but only those with an international licence and riding experience should consider it. Overall, Da Lat is an ideal destination for budget travellers.

The purpose of this proposal is to suggest how the funds available could be used to organise an event that brings students and local residents together. I propose holding a one-day Community Skills Fair on the college campus.

Flexible working hours
Allowing staff to start between 7.30 and 10 a.m. would help those with long commutes or childcare responsibilities. Several companies in our sector have introduced similar schemes with positive results.

A quiet room
The small meeting room on the third floor is rarely used and could easily be converted into a quiet space where employees can rest, meditate or simply take a break away from their desks.

I would also suggest a policy discouraging internal emails after 7 p.m., except in emergencies. This would send a clear message that time off is respected.

It is widely accepted that employees who feel rested and valued are more productive and less likely to take sick leave or leave the company. The moment I opened the envelope, I knew my life was about to change. Inside was a single faded photograph of a young woman standing outside a bakery in Paris – and she looked exactly like me.

The envelope had arrived that morning with no letter and no return address, only my name written in elegant, old-fashioned handwriting. At first, I assumed it was a joke. But when I showed the photo to my grandmother, the colour drained from her face.

'Where did you get this?' she whispered. For a long time she said nothing. Then, slowly, she began to tell me a story she had kept secret for fifty years: she had had a twin sister, who had stayed in France when the rest of the family moved to Vietnam. They had lost contact after an argument and never spoken again.

My confusion gradually turned into excitement. Somewhere, there was a whole branch of my family I had never known existed. Three months later, I was standing outside that same bakery, holding the photograph, when an elderly woman stepped out of the door and smiled at me.

It was supposed to be a gentle day's hiking. Minh and I had planned the trip for months, so when the park ranger mentioned that a storm might arrive in the afternoon, we simply laughed it off. The sky was perfectly blue, after all.

By midday, we had reached the top of the ridge and were enjoying the spectacular view. That was when we noticed the dark clouds racing towards us. Within minutes, the temperature dropped sharply, and the first drops of rain turned into a violent downpour. The path, which had been dry and easy that morning, became a river of mud.

We tried to hurry down, but Minh slipped and twisted his ankle badly. Soaked and shivering, we sheltered under a rocky overhang while lightning lit up the valley below. My phone had no signal, and I began to wonder whether anyone would find us before dark.

Hours later, we saw torches moving up the hill. The ranger, realising we hadn't returned, had sent out a search team. He didn't say 'I told you so', but he didn't need to – and that was the last time I ever ignored a weather warning.

It was pouring with rain when Lan noticed the elderly man at the bus stop. He was staring helplessly at a timetable, clutching a crumpled piece of paper with an address on it. Everyone else was hurrying past, heads down, eyes on their phones.

Lan was already late for work, but something made her stop. The man, it turned out, had just arrived from the countryside to visit his son in hospital and had no idea which bus to take. Instead of simply pointing the way, Lan decided to go with him. She shared her umbrella, paid his fare and walked him right to the hospital entrance.

She arrived at the office forty minutes late, soaking wet, and thought no more about it.

Six months later, Lan was invited to a job interview at a company she had always dreamed of working for. As she walked into the room, the interviewer looked up, paused, and broke into a broad smile. 'I believe you met my father once,' he said. 'He's never stopped talking about the young woman who got him to the hospital.'

Dear Ms Wong,

Thank you for your email. I am happy to give some feedback on the Digital Marketing course, which I completed last week.

Overall, I found the course extremely worthwhile. The most useful part was undoubtedly the module on data analysis, as it gave me practical skills that I have already started using in my job. The weekly live sessions with the tutor were also very helpful, since they gave us the chance to ask questions and learn from other participants.

There were, however, one or two problems. Some of the video lectures had poor sound quality, and on several occasions the quizzes did not save my answers, which was rather frustrating.

For future courses, I would suggest providing written summaries of each lecture so that participants can review the key points more easily. It might also be worth including more real-life case studies.

Thank you again for a valuable experience.

Dear Editor,

I am writing in response to your article of 3 May about the council's plan to replace Green Hill Park with a multi-storey car park. As a resident of the area for over twenty years, I am deeply concerned about this proposal.

The park is far more than an empty space waiting to be developed. It is where children play after school, elderly residents meet for exercise each morning and families gather at weekends. In a neighbourhood where most people live in flats, it is the only green space within walking distance.

The council argues that a car park is needed to support local shops. While I recognise that parking is a problem, building more spaces will simply encourage more traffic and pollution. Moreover, once the park is gone, it will be gone forever.

A far better solution would be to improve bus services into the town centre and create a park-and-ride scheme on the empty land near the motorway. This would reduce congestion without sacrificing one of our most valuable community assets.

As cities become increasingly congested, some urban planners have proposed banning cars from city centres altogether. While this idea has clear benefits, I believe a total ban would be impractical in most cities.

The most obvious advantage would be a reduction in air pollution, which is responsible for thousands of premature deaths every year. City centres without cars would also be quieter and safer for pedestrians and cyclists, encouraging people to walk more and improving public health.

On the other hand, many businesses depend on customers who arrive by car, as well as on deliveries. Shop owners in some cities that have restricted traffic have reported a fall in sales, at least initially. A complete ban could therefore damage the very areas it was intended to improve.

It is also important to consider people with disabilities and the elderly, for whom using public transport or walking long distances may be extremely difficult.

In my view, a more balanced approach would be to restrict private cars during peak hours, introduce congestion charges and invest heavily in public transport. Only when reliable alternatives exist will people be willing to leave their cars at home.

Young people today follow the lives of famous people more closely than ever before, thanks largely to social media. This raises the question of whether celebrities should be expected to set a good example. In my opinion, they do have some responsibility, but expectations should be realistic.

There is no denying that celebrities have enormous influence. When a famous singer promotes a product or expresses a view, millions of teenagers may copy them. Given this power, it seems reasonable to expect them to avoid encouraging dangerous or irresponsible behaviour, such as extreme dieting.

However, it is unfair to demand that celebrities be perfect. They are human beings who make mistakes like everyone else, and many of them became famous for their talent, not because they wanted to be role models. Constant public criticism of their private lives can also be extremely damaging to their mental health.

Moreover, I believe parents and teachers play a far more important role in shaping young people's values than celebrities do.

In conclusion, while celebrities should use their influence responsibly, it is ultimately up to families and schools to teach young people how to think critically about the people they admire.

items.promptVi: 'Du lịch gây hại nhiều hơn lợi cho cộng đồng địa phương.' Hãy viết bài luận nêu ý kiến.
points: the effect on culture and the environment
items.sampleAnswer:
Tourism is one of the world's largest industries, yet its impact on local communities is increasingly being questioned. Although mass tourism can undoubtedly cause problems, I do not believe it does more harm than good, provided it is properly managed.

From an economic point of view, tourism brings considerable benefits. It creates jobs in hotels, restaurants and transport, and it allows small businesses such as craft shops and family-run guesthouses to flourish. In many rural areas, it is one of the few sources of income available.

Nevertheless, the negative effects cannot be ignored. Popular destinations often suffer from overcrowding, rising property prices and pollution. In some places, traditional festivals and crafts have been turned into performances for visitors, losing much of their original meaning.

What matters most, in my view, is how tourism is controlled. Limiting visitor numbers at fragile sites, ensuring that profits stay within the local community and involving residents in decision-making can greatly reduce the harm.

In conclusion, tourism is neither entirely positive nor entirely negative. When it is planned with local people in mind, its benefits can clearly outweigh its costs.
